stem: Which of the following nitrogenous wastes is the most toxic and is excreted mainly by aquatic animals?
hint: Think of the waste that needs the most water to flush out safely.
explanation: Step 1: Nitrogenous wastes differ in toxicity — ammonia > urea > uric acid. Step 2: Ammonia is highly toxic and soluble, so it must be diluted in large volumes of water. Step 3: Aquatic animals (many bony fishes, amphibian tadpoles) excrete ammonia directly and are called ammonotelic.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.0 Introduction)

stem: Humans are ureotelic. What does this mean?

options.text: They excrete urea as the main nitrogenous waste
They excrete uric acid as pellets
They do not excrete nitrogenous waste

hint: Ureo- points to the waste humans mainly produce.
explanation: Step 1: 'Ureotelic' comes from urea. Step 2: Mammals (including humans), marine fishes and many amphibians convert toxic ammonia into less toxic urea in the liver. Step 3: Urea is then filtered out by the kidneys and excreted in urine.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.0 Introduction)

stem: Which group of animals is uricotelic, excreting nitrogenous waste mainly as uric acid?
hint: Think of animals that lay shelled eggs on land and must conserve water.
explanation: Step 1: Uric acid is the least toxic and least soluble nitrogenous waste, excreted as a paste with minimal water loss. Step 2: This suits animals with limited water — birds, reptiles and insects. Step 3: They are called uricotelic.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.0 Introduction)

stem: In humans, urea is mainly synthesised in which organ?
hint: The organ that also detoxifies blood and makes bile.
explanation: Step 1: Ammonia from protein metabolism is toxic and must be converted. Step 2: This conversion happens through the ornithine (urea) cycle. Step 3: The urea cycle operates in the liver; urea then travels in blood to the kidneys for excretion.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.0 Introduction)

stem: Urine formed in the kidney reaches the urinary bladder through the:
hint: Two muscular tubes, one from each kidney, carry urine down.
explanation: Step 1: Urine collects in the renal pelvis of each kidney. Step 2: From there it flows down a pair of thin muscular tubes. Step 3: These ureters carry urine to the urinary bladder (the urethra carries it out of the body).
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the:
hint: One word: the microscopic tubule where urine is actually formed.
explanation: Step 1: Each kidney contains about a million microscopic filtering units. Step 2: Each unit — glomerulus plus its renal tubule — filters blood and forms urine. Step 3: This unit is the nephron, the structural and functional unit of the kidney.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: Approximately how many nephrons does each human kidney contain?
hint: More than a lakh, far fewer than a crore.
explanation: Step 1: Nephrons are microscopic, so a kidney packs in a very large number. Step 2: NCERT states each kidney has nearly one million nephrons. Step 3: This huge number gives the kidney its enormous filtering surface.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: The glomerulus is best described as:
hint: Think of a tiny ball of blood vessels where filtration begins.
explanation: Step 1: Blood enters the nephron through the afferent arteriole. Step 2: Inside Bowman's capsule this arteriole branches into a tuft of capillaries. Step 3: This capillary tuft is the glomerulus — the site of blood filtration.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: Bowman's capsule is:

options.text: The funnel that collects urine from many nephrons
A double-walled cup enclosing the glomerulus
The U-shaped part of the tubule
The outer region of the kidney

hint: It cups the glomerulus like a catcher's mitt.
explanation: Step 1: The nephron begins with the glomerulus. Step 2: Around it sits a double-walled, cup-shaped structure. Step 3: This is Bowman's capsule; together with the glomerulus it forms the renal (Malpighian) corpuscle where filtrate collects.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: Which region of the kidney is the outer zone?
hint: Cortex is to the kidney what bark is to a tree — the outer layer.
explanation: Step 1: A longitudinal section of the kidney shows two zones. Step 2: The outer zone is the cortex and the inner zone is the medulla. Step 3: The medulla is divided into cone-shaped medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is the site where:

options.text: Nearly all glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed
Urine is finally concentrated under ADH

hint: The PCT does the bulk of the reclaiming work — including 100% of glucose.
explanation: Step 1: Filtrate entering the PCT still contains useful substances like glucose and amino acids. Step 2: The PCT reabsorbs nearly all of the glucose and amino acids plus about 65% of water and Na+. Step 3: Its cells have brush-border microvilli to maximise reabsorption surface.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: The loop of Henle plays its main role in:

options.text: Concentrating urine via the counter-current mechanism

hint: Its U-shape in the medulla builds the salt gradient that concentrates urine.
explanation: Step 1: The loop of Henle dips into the medulla with descending and ascending limbs. Step 2: Together with the vasa recta it operates a counter-current mechanism that maintains a high salt concentration in the medullary interstitium. Step 3: This gradient lets the kidney produce concentrated urine and conserve water.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: Which of the following substances is normally NOT found in the glomerular filtrate?
hint: Filtration lets small molecules through — but not cells.
explanation: Step 1: The glomerular filtration membrane allows water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, urea, ions) to pass. Step 2: Cells and large plasma proteins are too big to cross. Step 3: So red blood cells are absent from normal filtrate; their presence in urine indicates a problem.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately:
hint: About an eighth of a litre every minute.
explanation: Step 1: GFR is the volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute. Step 2: In a healthy adult it is about 125 mL per minute. Step 3: That is roughly 180 litres of filtrate per day, of which only ~1–1.5 L leaves as urine.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: Glomerular filtration is driven mainly by:
hint: Blood pressure pushes fluid out of the capillaries.
explanation: Step 1: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so pressure builds in the glomerulus. Step 2: This hydrostatic pressure forces water and small solutes across the filtration membrane. Step 3: It is opposed by osmotic pressure and capsular pressure, but the net filtration pressure stays positive.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: Tubular secretion is the process by which:

options.text: Useful substances are reabsorbed into blood
Unwanted substances move from blood into the tubule
Water is conserved in the medulla

hint: Secretion is the opposite direction to reabsorption — into the tubule, out of the body.
explanation: Step 1: Besides filtration and reabsorption, the nephron actively moves some substances from peritubular capillaries into the tubular fluid. Step 2: These include H+, K+, ammonia and certain drugs. Step 3: This tubular secretion helps eliminate wastes and fine-tune blood pH.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: ADH (vasopressin) increases urine concentration by:

options.text: Increasing water reabsorption in the collecting duct

hint: ADH = anti-diuretic = less water lost as urine.
explanation: Step 1: When the body is dehydrated, the hypothalamus releases ADH. Step 2: ADH makes the collecting duct walls more permeable to water. Step 3: More water is reabsorbed into the blood, so a smaller volume of concentrated urine is produced.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.3 Function of the Tubules)

stem: Aldosterone acts mainly on which part of the nephron to regulate Na+?

options.text: Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct

hint: The 'late' segments fine-tune salt under hormonal control.
explanation: Step 1: Aldosterone is released by the adrenal cortex when blood Na+ is low. Step 2: It acts on the DCT and collecting duct. Step 3: It increases Na+ reabsorption (and water follows), raising blood volume and pressure.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.3 Function of the Tubules)

stem: The vasa recta is:

options.text: A network of capillaries around the loop of Henle
The tube carrying urine to the bladder
A hormone secreted by the kidney

hint: 'Recta' = straight — straight capillaries running alongside the loop.
explanation: Step 1: The loop of Henle is surrounded by a special capillary network. Step 2: These long, straight capillaries are the vasa recta. Step 3: Together with the loop they maintain the medullary salt gradient via counter-current exchange.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: Which cells of the PCT have a brush border that increases reabsorptive surface area?
hint: Microvilli = microscopic brushes on the tubule lining.
explanation: Step 1: The PCT must reabsorb huge amounts of solute and water. Step 2: Its lining of cuboidal epithelial cells bears dense microvilli — the brush border. Step 3: This enormously increases surface area for reabsorption; podocytes instead line Bowman's capsule.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: The process of expelling urine from the bladder is called:
hint: The technical term for urination.
explanation: Step 1: Urine stored in the bladder stretches its wall, triggering a reflex. Step 2: The detrusor muscle contracts and the sphincter relaxes. Step 3: This neural reflex expelling urine is called micturition.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.4 Mechanism of Concentration of the Filtrate)

stem: An average healthy adult excretes about how much urine per day?
hint: Far less than the 180 L filtered — most water is reclaimed.
explanation: Step 1: About 180 L of filtrate forms daily. Step 2: Roughly 99% of the water is reabsorbed along the tubules. Step 3: Only about 1–1.5 L is finally excreted as urine per day.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: The pH of normal human urine is approximately:
hint: Slightly acidic — around six.
explanation: Step 1: Blood pH is tightly held near 7.4, and the kidney excretes excess H+. Step 2: This makes urine mildly acidic on average. Step 3: Normal urine pH is about 6.0 (range roughly 4.5–8 depending on diet).
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.5 Regulation of Kidney Function)

stem: Kidney stones most commonly form from crystallised deposits of:
hint: The commonest stone salt pairs calcium with oxalate.
explanation: Step 1: When urine becomes supersaturated, salts can crystallise in the kidney. Step 2: The most frequent stones are calcium oxalate (also calcium phosphate, uric acid). Step 3: This condition is called nephrolithiasis; small stones may pass, large ones need treatment.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.6 Disorders of the Excretory System)

stem: Uremia refers to:

options.text: Abnormally high urea in the blood

hint: Ur-emia: urea in the blood (haemia).
explanation: Step 1: When kidneys fail, they cannot clear urea from blood. Step 2: Urea accumulates to harmful levels — a condition called uremia. Step 3: It is treated by hemodialysis (artificial kidney) or kidney transplant.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.6 Disorders of the Excretory System)

stem: In hemodialysis, urea is removed from blood because:

options.text: Urea diffuses across a semipermeable membrane into dialysing fluid
The liver converts it to ammonia

hint: Dialysis works on simple diffusion down a concentration gradient.
explanation: Step 1: The patient's blood flows on one side of a cellophane (semipermeable) membrane. Step 2: Dialysing fluid with the same composition as plasma minus wastes flows on the other side. Step 3: Urea and excess ions diffuse out of blood into the fluid; cells and proteins are too large to cross.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.6 Disorders of the Excretory System)

stem: Which part of the nephron is primarily responsible for the reabsorption of bicarbonate (HCO3−) and thus blood pH balance?
hint: The PCT reclaims the bulk of filtered bicarbonate.
explanation: Step 1: Bicarbonate buffers blood pH and is freely filtered. Step 2: About 80–90% of filtered HCO3− is reabsorbed in the PCT. Step 3: This reclamation is central to the kidney's role in acid–base balance.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.3 Function of the Tubules)

stem: The renal pelvis is:

options.text: The outer zone of the kidney
A funnel-shaped space collecting urine from calyces
The functional unit of the kidney
A blood vessel entering the kidney

hint: Pelvis = basin; it gathers urine before the ureter.
explanation: Step 1: Urine from collecting ducts drains through papillae into minor and major calyces. Step 2: The calyces open into a broad funnel-shaped cavity. Step 3: This renal pelvis narrows into the ureter, which carries urine to the bladder.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.1 Human Excretory System)

stem: Which of the following is a correct match of nephron part to its main function?

options.text: Loop of Henle — filtration of blood

hint: Match each part to what it actually does.
explanation: Step 1: Glomerulus filters (not reabsorbs); loop of Henle concentrates (does not filter). Step 2: The PCT reabsorbs nearly all glucose/amino acids and most water and salts. Step 3: Urea is made in the liver, not the collecting duct — so only the PCT match is correct.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.2 Urine Formation)

stem: Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is formed by cellular modifications of:

options.text: The DCT and the afferent arteriole
The collecting duct and vasa recta

hint: It sits where the DCT passes between the two arterioles of its own glomerulus.
explanation: Step 1: As the DCT loops back, it passes between the afferent and efferent arterioles. Step 2: Here, DCT cells become macula densa and arteriole cells become juxtaglomerular cells. Step 3: This JGA senses blood pressure and Na+ levels and regulates GFR and renin release.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 19 — Excretory Products and Their Elimination (§19.5 Regulation of Kidney Function)
